detail.title: Creditor Rights and Investment Efficiency in Financially Distressed Firms
detail.abstract: Do strong creditor rights in bankruptcy law improve the efficiency of investments in financially distressed firms? Exploiting a landmark insolvency resolution reform, we find that strengthening creditor-control rights improves the investment efficiency of financially distressed firms compared to non-distressed firms by reducing their overinvestment. Further, stronger creditor rights are more effective in improving the investment efficiency of firms with higher personal costs of bankruptcy of shareholders and less disciplined managers. Fear of sub-optimal liquidation, loss of control over the firm, and management turnover in the event of insolvency in a regime with stronger creditor rights incentivizes managers and shareholders of distressed firms to utilize resources more efficiently. These results provide robust evidence on the economic mechanisms via which bankruptcy laws can address agency problems in principal-agent models with information asymmetry.

detail.abstract: This study investigates the convergence of greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions between two structurally distinct European regions: Eastern Europe, consisting of transition economies, and Northern Europe, composed of advanced economies. The analysis employs panel regressions (fixed effects and 2SLS), including interaction variables to capture the complex relationships among the examined factors.The results highlight significant regional disparities. In both clusters, GDP growth is positively correlated with GHG emissions, confirming the persistence of scale effects and contradicting the assumption of automatic decoupling in developed economies. Energy productivity systematically reduces emissions in both regions, underlining the universal role of efficiency. A strong synergistic effect is also observed between renewable energy use and improvements in energy productivity, amplifying emission reductions. However, differences emerge in the effectiveness of renewable integration and environmental taxation: while these instruments reduce emissions effectively in Nordic countries, their impact in Eastern economies is weaker or even counterproductive, reflecting lower institutional capacity and slower technological adoption.The paper makes an original contribution to the literature on ecological economics by demonstrating the heterogeneous effectiveness of climate policies between advanced and transition economies. It also provides practical recommendations for designing European strategies tailored to the specific institutional and developmental contexts of each region.

detail.abstract: National regulatory authorities (NRAs) in low-and middle-income countries (LMICs) need a steady stream of financing for pre-and post-market-entry regulation. detail.title: An Anatomy of the International Financial System Vis-À-Vis the Human Body System
detail.abstract:
This paper attempts to construct an anatomical structure around key constituents in the International Financial System (“IFS”) in comparison with anatomical features of the human body. The IFS is a conglomeration of financial systems, encompassing financial and monetary activities, that are so intertwined that the fragility of a system, affects the stability of the IFS. Similarly, the human body system is a compendium of sub-systems working together to ensure the body functions effectively. The human body and IFS are both products of a complicated intertwined formation of sub-systems. Thus, analogies are made between the structure and functions of key constituents in the IFS, and vital organs and components in seven (7) systems of the human body; circulatory, respiratory, digestive, nervous, skeletal, integumentary, and respiratory systems.

The contextual structure of this paper is twofold: (1) making analogies between constituents of the IFS and components of the human body system, (2) positing supporting evidence to the analogies through occurrences from select global financial crises, and a global pandemic. The global financial crises are: The Great Depression (1929-1939), The International Debt Crisis (1982-1989), The Asian Financial Crisis (1997-1999), and The Great Recession (2007-2009). The global pandemic is the COVID-19 pandemic (2019-till date).

detail.title: Economic and Financial Solutions for Biodiversity Conservation
detail.abstract: Economic and financial instruments have been widely applied in biodiversity conservation, from payments for ecosystem services to green bonds, from biodiversity offsets to Nature Positive frameworks-these market-based mechanisms continue to innovate and expand. However, despite the continuous growth in funding scale and instrument diversity, global biodiversity continues to decline at an accelerating pace. This paper systematically analyzes the operational mechanisms and implementation outcomes of major conservation instruments, finding that their widespread failure stems from fundamental contradictions between market logic and ecosystem characteristics. These contradictions manifest in three aspects: ecological values cannot be fully monetized, ecological losses are often irreversible, and the market's demand for short-term returns conflicts with the long-term processes of ecological restoration. Facing the limitations of traditional instruments, emerging global frameworks such as Nature Positive, while offering conceptual innovations, perpetuate the inherent deficiencies of marketbased approaches. In light of this, this paper proposes systematic reform pathways, including value pluralization, incentive mechanism restructuring, spatiotemporal scale integration, democratization of power relations, and economic model transformation, emphasizing that transcending market-based thinking is key to achieving effective conservation.

detail.title: The Evolution of Trumpism: Economic Policy Shifts from the 45th to the 47th Presidency in the Shadow of Biden's Legacy
detail.abstract: This paper examines the transformation of Donald Trump's economic policies between his first term (2017-2021) and his second term (2025-present), with a particular focus on how Joe Biden's presidency (2021-2025) served as a pivotal catalyst for change. Drawing on economic data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) and Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA), as well as analyses from institutions like the Tax Foundation and Penn Wharton Budget Model, the study highlights Biden's inflation crisis-peaking at 9.1% in 2022-as a key factor enabling Trump's bolder approach in 2025. While Trump's core principles of tax reduction, deregulation, and protectionism remain consistent, his second term features amplified tariffs (10-20% universal, 60% on China) that function as demand-suppressing mechanisms, contributing to stabilized inflation around 2.4% by mid-2025. Comparative analysis reveals a shift from experimental policies in the 45th presidency to more aggressive, less constrained actions in the 47th, facilitated by Republican congressional control and public disillusionment with Biden's fiscal overreach. The paper argues that this evolution reflects broader populist responses to post-pandemic economic anxieties, with implications for future U.S. fiscal stability and global trade. Findings suggest Trump's tariffs may yield short-term revenue gains ($93.9 billion by June 2025) but risk long-term GDP reductions (up to 6%), underscoring the tension between protectionism and growth.

detail.abstract: Central banking has historically been male-dominated. Few women held leadership roles in central banking until recently, and the profession's sine qua non of leadership attributes-inflation aversion-is male-coded in the public imagination. Research shows that, as a result, the women who do become central bankers encounter gender-incongruence costs in the form of reduced public support. What might ameliorate those costs? We propose that female role models can do so by shifting social expectations of central banking's implicit "maleness," and thus improving how the public perceives female central bankers. Knowing about one female central banker improves people's perceptions of others. We test our theory using survey experiments in the eurozone that randomly attribute central bank communication to male and female central bankers. Our findings show that European respondents who are aware of female central bank leaders respond more favorably to communications attributed to other, less prominent female central bankers that we presented to them.

detail.abstract: This paper investigates how the global dominance of the US dollar amplifies the cross-border transmission of financial shocks originating in the United States. I develop a small open economy DSGE model that embeds the dollar’s central role in international trade and finance and calibrate it to the Korean economy. Key parameters are estimated by matching impulse responses to a shock in the excess bond premium (EBP), a standard measure of US financial conditions. The analysis shows that two core functions of the dollar in global finance—the role of dollar-denominated bonds as safe assets and the dollar’s centrality in financing working capital for global supply chains—constitute the primary channels through which US financial shocks spill over internationally. Absent these mechanisms, the output losses from US financial shocks would be more than two-thirds smaller. Finally, the results suggest that shifting trade invoicing from the dollar to the domestic currency can significantly dampen these spillovers as well, lowering the output losses by roughly one-fourth.

detail.abstract:
Russia’s invasion of Ukraine altered the structure and the fundamentals of post-Cold War security architecture. In more than one sense, it appeared unequivocally that few things shall remain untarnished in matters pertaining to the order of state-to-state interactions or the (crumbling) self-desired universality of international law. But such a metamorphosis of perception did not limit to issues of high politics, military doctrine or legal responsibility in times of war.

Simultaneously with Russia’s terrestrial deployment of large-scale destruction upon its neighbor, a naval blockade was instituted, effectively sealing all of Ukraine’s (remaining) Black Sea ports from their commerce with the wider world. More than 20 tons of agricultural products – headed for export – remained grounded in the docks and inland silos, unable to reach global markets. Then followed a systematic campaign of incapacitating Ukraine’s grain-producing sector: dismantling of infrastructure, theft of stocked harvests, removal of equipment and industrial hardware.

The whole world witnessed Russia’s (ab)use of famine as a threat aimed not merely at Ukraine, but to the entire array of Kyiv’s customers overseas. And, in this sense, the present study will proceed by explaining the two actors’ centrality and relevance in the global food supply chains. Further on, it will address the manner in which the war changed both their positions and those of regular overseas customers, leading to a race to buy and stock on a disrupted market. In the final parts, the short- and medium-term solutions to the crisis will be analyzed, struggling to glimpse the new ‘horizon’ of food supply and the larger global market in the aftermath of the blockade.

With or without the blockade, a significant part of the transnational agricultural export capacity had been affected by Russia’s invasion, proving that wars (and their subsequent effects) cannot be ‘grounded’ and ‘isolated’. What happens in Ukraine, might not stay in Ukraine, but provoke hunger across the other side of the globe.

detail.abstract: This study analyzes the determinants of rural Congolese households' adherence to Payment for Environmental Services (PES) programs through two contrasting cases: PIREDD Kwilu, a "top-down" provincial program, and SACKEN in Kingakati, a "bottom-up" community initiative. Based on a survey of 549 households, supplemented by interviews and focus groups, it uses econometric models (Probit, IV-Probit, Heckman, IVREG2) to correct for endogeneity and selection biases.The results first indicate that, paradoxically, high dependence on forest resources discourages participation in the absence of economic alternatives. On the other hand, targeted awareness-raising, secure land titles and payment levels are essential levers for offsetting the opportunity cost of unsustainable practices. Local institutional anchoring, measured by participation in community work, agricultural seniority and indigenous membership, significantly reinforces the effectiveness of incentives, especially in the case of SACKEN.The heterogeneity of effects reveals that forest dependency results in an increase in membership of the "bottom-up" model, while PIREDD membership figures remain lower. Furthermore, factors such as levels of formal education and gender-moderated participation differ according to the governance scale, with a quarter of households perceiving no benefit at all. The major obstacles are late payment, inadequate input quality and distribution, reduced farmland and insufficient social support. To guarantee take-up, it is recommended to calibrate PES schemes according to the level of forest dependency, to adapt communication to educational and gender profiles, and to rely on community networks.

detail.abstract: Current application of US antitrust law is at odds with common sense. The US v Google LLC decision provides a prime example. Apple extracts billions of dollars annually from Google, yet antitrust agencies and courts identify Google as the monopolist. The reason for this error lies in the underdeveloped state of monopoly maintenance doctrine. Following Microsoft, the law allows plaintiffs to charge dominant firms with violations of Section 2 of the Sherman Act for conduct responsive to monopoly power exploitation by a trading partner. detail.abstract:
In this article, Pomp examines Quad Graphics v. North Carolina Department of Revenue, where the North Carolina Supreme Court upheld an assessment of over $3 million in sales tax and penalties on a Wisconsin-based company for printed materials shipped into North Carolina. To uphold the assessment, the North Carolina Supreme Court effectively overruled the 1944 U.S. Supreme Court case of McLeod v. J.E. Dilworth Co., which had prohibited states from applying sales tax to transactions consummated out of state under facts essentially identical to those in Quad.

The Quad court thought that Complete Auto Transit v. Brady and South Dakota v. Wayfair Inc. had implicitly overruled Dilworth, but the article argues this is mistaken. Cases such as National Geographic Society v. California Board of Equalization, which was decided less than a month after Complete Auto, and Oklahoma Tax Commission v. Jefferson Lines, which was cited repeatedly in Quad, demonstrate that the Supreme Court continued to accept Dilworth after Complete Auto. Moreover, the taxpayers in Wayfair never raised a Dilworth argument. They had no incentive to do so because it would have delayed the resolution of the more pressing state attack on the physical presence requirement. Thus, Wayfair cannot be read as overturning Dilworth.

The article warns of Quad’s unintended consequences for Native American tribes and their members. In some states, state sales taxes are considered a vendor levy, with the legal incidence falling on vendors (retailers), unlike use taxes, which fall on the purchasers. Because states cannot impose use taxes on tribes or tribal members for on-reservation purchases, shifting from use taxes to vendor-based sales taxes could raise costs for tribes. This issue is particularly concerning in states like North Carolina and South Dakota, which impose vendor-based sales taxes.

If the U.S. Supreme Court declines review of Quad, and more states follow North Carolina in ignoring Dilworth, tribes may face significant financial impacts. The article concludes that tribes should be on alert for this impending problem.

detail.abstract: We investigate profit-share auctions in a procurement context, comparing them with traditional cash auctions to identify which mechanism yields lower expenses for buyers. We also explore whether specifying a high project value in profit-share auction contracts influences supplier bidding behavior. Using theoretical analysis and experimental methods, we observe that profit-share auctions lead to lower buyer expenses compared to traditional cash auctions. Furthermore, we find that the buyer benefits from specifying a high project value in the contract, as this commitment induces more aggressive bidding from the suppliers. While profit-share auctions result in significantly lower buyer expenses than cash auctions, the observed differences are smaller than predicted. This discrepancy is due to (i) more pronounced underbidding in cash auctions and (ii) lower efficiency in profit-share auctions caused by noisy bidding. Our findings suggest that managers can reduce procurement costs by adopting profit-share auctions and strategically committing to a high project value in contracts. However, they should be aware that real-world savings may be smaller than theoretically predicted due to supplier bidding behavior.

detail.abstract:
In “Strike with Pride”: Unionizing as an LGBTQ Rights Strategy, a remarkable wave of organizing at Starbucks tests two pillars of work law: the anti-discrimination precepts of Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, and the labor activism protections afforded even earlier under the National Labor Relations Act (NLRA). Amid waves of workers who struck retailers, Hollywood studios, express-mail facilities, and automaker assembly lines in recent years—Professor Leonore Carpenter examines how, for low-wage LGBTQ workers, Title VII’s legal structures disincentivize private enforcement and can scarcely compete with the solidarism and power-shifting the NLRA was intended to protect. The baristas’ latest “Strike with Pride” campaign trained a national spotlight on workers realizing radically different ways of operating, defying the stereotype of unionizing drives focused only on economic terms of employment. Carpenter’s argument is persuasive, richly documented, and illuminates how unions bear the brunt of mediating identities, particularly queer workers whose right to exist remain in dire contention.

Our Essay responds from the vantage point of a new presidential administration, one openly antagonistic toward LGBTQIA+ communities, and a Roberts Court unwilling to recognize that a state law banning gender-affirming care—core medical treatments received by transgender youth—warrants constitutional heightened scrutiny. [ ] The unrest that spurred a renaissance of new, intersectional organizing models is particularly poignant as U.S. society is increasingly marred by hyperpolarization and steep corrosion of the rule of law. Acknowledging anti-queer violence and other attacks on communities’ security, her analysis arrives amid dramatic changes within the broader literature—in workplace diversity, rising awareness of the dynamics between identities and movements, and greater disillusionment with economic policies.

Accordingly, this Essay advances three main responses to Carpenter’s important critiques. The first two are structural, addressing the nested dualities that drive Carpenter’s analysis. The third is in the vein of expanding the critical legal traditions Strike with Pride invokes to meet additional challenges.

In Part I, we argue that the modern interplay between Title VII and NLRA is complex, and the expressive effects of each law are more difficult to measure. In that vein, we advance the claim that centering the needs of LGBTQ workers in low-paying professions warrants more extended focus on members’ needs within unions and campaigns. In Part II, we argue that the impacts of Title VII and Bostock warrants more extensive examination. Finally, in Part III we advance the claim that twenty-first century labor organizing, when intersectional and fully inclusive in its solidarity, will build power even during a time of economic retrenchment.

detail.abstract: Several papers highlight the demise of momentum in U.S. equity markets in recent decades. Our analysis finds significant abnormal returns from 6-month momentum, but lack thereof from 12month and price-to-high momentum. We construct double-sorted portfolios to isolate 12-month and price-to-high effects. detail.abstract: For hundreds of years, Geneva has been regarded as a “City of Peace” or the “Capital of Peace.” This directly stems from Geneva’s role as one of the most significant centers for peace negotiations in modern history, as well as Geneva’s location in Switzerland, the country with the oldest policy of neutrality and non-alignment in the world. However, since the outbreak of the Ukraine War, Geneva has slowly begun to lose its grip on the title of “City of Peace” as other cities in the world have risen to meet the challenge of hosting peace talks between belligerent nations or factions. This is due to a variety of factors. First, Switzerland appeared to abandon its centuries-long neutrality policy, in which it refused to take sides in the First or Second World Wars or the Cold War, by sanctioning Russia in 2022 for its aggression in Ukraine. Another issue that has led to Geneva’s diminishing stature as a “City of Peace” is that the “center of gravity” of global politics has shifted from the “West” to the “Global South.” Thus, this article compares and contrasts three cities that have emerged to rival Geneva as hosts of peace summits, namely Istanbul, Doha, and Singapore, before predicting the diplomatic role that these cities will play in the future.

detail.abstract: Background/Objectives: Burnout is associated with difficulties in daily executive functions and alterations in the underlying neural processes. Therefore, this study aims to examine the Relationship between burnout and cognitive functioning, and identify the key factors influencing this connection.Materials and Methods : 102 volunteers from a Moroccan industrial company underwent two neurocognitive digital tests using the ELIAN software and completed the self-administered "Maslach Burnout Inventory: MBI" questionnaire. Results : The average scores for visuospatial perception, visual working memory, execution time, processing speed, and concentration capacity tended to be higher among employees identified as exhausted. However, a statistically significant association with burnout was observed only for visuospatial perception (p = 0.008). In contrast, the average precision score showed a slight, non-significant decline in the exhausted group in the overall sample. Notably, this decline reached statistical significance (p = 0.011) when considering only women. Similarly, a significant association between burnout and enhanced concentration capacity was found in women (p = 0.037). Among participants with a lower educational level, processing speed appeared to improve under burnout (p = 0.057). Additionally, visuospatial perception scores were significantly higher in exhausted participants under the age of 40 (p = 0.028). These patterns suggest that factors such as age, gender, and educational level may influence the relationship between burnout and cognitive functions. Conclusion : The findings of our study suggest that the association between burnout and cognitive functions may vary depending on individual characteristics, the severity of burnout, and the nature of the cognitive functions assessed.

detail.abstract: As nations transition to a circular economy, their association with waste must be rectified. The obligation for waste collection, segregation, and disposal has traditionally been regarded as the duty of municipalities and public authorities. In a linear economy, the accountability of producers and manufacturers was confined to the duration of the product's utilisation. A circular economy mandates circularity in product design and disposal. Extended producer responsibility (EPR) underscores the significant role of producers in the ecologically responsible management of waste from their products. It compels them to develop their products with eco-efficiency in mind. An EPR policy can significantly alter how waste is managed. As India prepares to transition into a circular economy, it becomes crucial to analyse the EPR rules. The study performs a documentary examination of all statutory regulations in India that embody the notion of EPR. The research paper aims to examine the implementation of mandatory EPR within the Indian legal framework to date, to pinpoint the principal sectors where mandatory EPR has been established in India, and to juxtapose the EPR framework in India with the guidance manual on EPR from the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD). The research indicated that EPR was first implemented in India in 2011 for plastics and electronic trash. India has an EPR framework for eight specific waste categories: plastic packaging, electronic trash, waste tires, battery waste, spent oil, end-of-life vehicles, building and demolition debris, and non-ferrous metals. When matched with the checklist for EPR policy contained in the OECD guidance manual, it was found that EPR rules presently in force in India substantially comply with the same. The paper thus concludes with the thought that the effectiveness of the EPR framework would greatly depend on the proper implementation of these rules.

detail.abstract:
This paper explores the learning and collaboration that can emerge when a postsecondary course is delivered using a dual-language approach: English and learners' first language, in this case, Spanish. Drawing from Berry’s (1992) Acculturation Theory, this study examines how offering a course in learners’ home language and in English at the same time can foster academic success, cultural affirmation, and a sense of belonging. It also provides a deeper conceptual understanding for Spanish-speaking early childhood educators studying in Canada.

The pedagogical strategy of translanguaging (García & Wei, 2014) was embedded in the course design, allowing learners to fluidly navigate between English and Spanish. The study is grounded in a qualitative ethnographic approach, incorporating narratives and reflections from two cohorts of learners enrolled in a 22-week online course to learn about Flight: Alberta’s Early Learning and Care Framework (Makovichuk et al., 2014). Participants included a total of 24 Spanish-speaking educators working in licensed early learning programs across Alberta, Canada. This project took place within two sections of this same course throughout the fall semester of 2024 and the winter semester of 2025. The research team working on this particular project consisted of the principal investigator, two course instructors, a course facilitator, and a research assistant.

Analysis of learner narratives revealed three central themes: language as a way of communicating, sharing a similar culture as a way of developing a sense of belonging, and professional learning as interconnected pathways to meaning- meaning. Participants emphasized that language and culture are inseparable from their learning process and professional identities. Particularly, learners identified interlinguistic benefits when engaging with course content in their home language, especially in English-dominant sectors. Additionally, participants currently employed in Spanish-language childcare centers reported feeling more confident in sharing course insights with colleagues, which reinforced their leadership and advocacy capacities.
This study highlights the potential of dual-language instruction to support culturally and linguistically diverse educators in Canadian higher education. While the course was limited to Spanish-speaking learners, we encourage future research to replicate and expand this model across other linguistic communities to validate and extend these findings.

detail.abstract: The data protection and data privacy framework in Pakistan in still in the initial stages, being scattered in the form of various draft bills and regulatory frameworks waiting to be a part of the legal system of Pakistan. This paper undertakes a critical assessment towards the efforts and steps taken in formulating a legal framework for data protection and data privacy. A comparative analysis will be made through evaluating the different data protection frameworks across jurisdictions such as Europe, India and the United States. This study assesses the key thematic areas, such as the legal grounds for processing, data rights, cross-border transfer of data, enforcement mechanisms, as well as technological competence in the era dominated by cloud computing and AI. Through outlining these jurisdictional strengths and drawbacks, the research would aim to highlight existing gaps in the draft legislations of Pakistan, such as ranging from vague provisions regarding enforcement to inadequate protection against cross-border data transfers or digital profiling. The paper attempts to propose a unified and comprehensive approach towards data protection regime, which is contextually relevant and sensitive for the legal system of Pakistan, through blending the rights-based approach from the EU, practical feasibility of the US, and the digital economy paradigm of India’s DPDP. Lastly, the paper suggests reforms for enhancing scalability, enforceability, as well as alignment of data protection framework with Pakistan’s constitutional framework and economic system. Therefore, this study aims to enrich the policy discourse through suggesting a clear roadmap for revamping the fragmented drafts on data protection laws, in the shape of a coherent, comprehensive and future-proof data protection law.

title: AI & the Future of Finance: A Framework for the Intelligent Financial Enterprise

detail.title: AI & the Future of Finance: A Framework for the Intelligent Financial Enterprise
detail.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is on track to transform finance more deeply than any shift since electronic markets first took hold. Yet, most conversations about "AI in finance" rarely move beyond surface-level themes-robotic process automation (RPA), predictive models, or packaged features bundled into systems like SAP or Oracle. This paper puts forward the Intelligent Financial Enterprise (IFE) framework, a model that differs sharply from these incremental tools. At its core is agentic AI with persistent memory-a step change from transactional algorithms that operate in isolation. Instead of producing one-off outputs, agentic AI absorbs an organization's financial history, decisions, and external context, using that cumulative understanding to provide guidance that is contextual, explainable, and forward-looking. The IFE is not another automation layer. It is an operating model built on three pillars: multi-agent collaboration, real-time orchestration of financial data, and decision-augmentation engines. Together, these elements allow finance leaders to move beyond reporting and automation toward continuous intelligence that reshapes treasury, FP&A, risk oversight, capital deployment, and even the way companies communicate with investors.

detail.abstract: This study introduces the concept of Significant Interpersonal Relationships (SIRs) as a unifying framework for understanding lethal violence. An empirical-inductive analysis of 357 homicides committed in Italy in 2017 identified 225 cases (62.7%) occurring within relational ties rather than criminal contexts. These included familial, intimate, intergenerational, and proximity relationships, bonds of trust and continuity that, paradoxically, emerge as the most lethal. Within this framework, the study advances four conceptual innovations: (1) proximity homicides, as an autonomous category that broadens analysis beyond family and intimate violence; (2) a unitary approach to suicides and homicide-suicides alongside domestic and gender-related violence, highlighting the continuum between despair and aggression; (3) maschicide, a category specular to femicide, drawing attention to male victims in gendered relational contexts such as rivalry and symbolic possession; and (4) coniunxicide, a neutral and precise term for partner killings, offered as an alternative to the gender-biased legal term uxoricidio. Findings reveal near symmetry between female (114) and male (111) victims and highlight systemic gaps in prevention policies when violence is framed solely through patriarchal or domestic lenses. The study calls for an expanded taxonomy situating gender-based violence within the broader field of relational violence.

detail.abstract: This paper examines the role of inventories in macroeconomic fluctuations across 29 European countries from 1999 to 2023, covering three major recessions. Using a novel panel dataset and dynamic panel-econometric methods, we analyse short- and long-run inventory behaviour. Results confirm the broadly pro-cyclical nature of inventories but reveal a more complex dynamic: inventories are initially depleted in response to demand shocks, followed by restocking and, in some cases, systematic correction after four quarters.During the Great Recession and Eurozone crisis, inventory depletion accounted for up to 80% of GDP losses, underscoring their amplifying role. In contrast, the COVID-19 recession featured limited de-stocking and earlier restocking, suggesting a structural shift in inventory strategies. These findings highlight inventories’ dual role—as amplifiers or stabilizers—depending on the timing and nature of shocks, and call for greater attention to inventory dynamics in forecasting and policy design.

detail.abstract: Purpose: This paper aims to present a new audit paradigm for identifying issues in organizational culture, which are the root causes of organizational misconduct and the ossification of management systems. This moves beyond the conventional framework of ISO internal audits, which tends to be limited to confirming "compliance" and "effectiveness." Design/methodology/approach: This is a conceptual study that integrates the "Two-Triangle Model (Commission/Omission)" and "Four Limits" frameworks from the author's previous research into the practical application of ISO internal auditing. It constructs a methodology to shift the audit's focus from "occurred nonconformities" to identifying "latent hazards (flaws or failures in processes)" that give rise to them, and presents the academic disciplines that form the intellectual foundation for identifying these hazards. Findings: Traditional internal audits tend to focus on pointing out rule violations (the results). However, by using the Two-Triangle Model (Commission/Omission) as an audit lens, it becomes possible to systematically evaluate more fundamental hazards. Furthermore, it has become clear that an interdisciplinary knowledge base, including social psychology, cognitive psychology, organizational behavior, failure analysis, and system safety engineering, is essential for auditors to detect these hazards in practice. Originality/value: The novelty of this paper lies in applying a theoretical framework from organizational misconduct research to the practice of ISO internal auditing. This paper operationalizes a two-track preventive strategy: Omission-First (directly reducing ignorance, unthinking, and irresponsibility) and Transition-Block (pre-empting the shift from omission to commission around organizational “triggers”), enabling detection of the compliant-but-harmful state. Research limitations/implications: The validity of qualitative hazard indicators (e.g., silence ratio, rationalization phrases) may be culture-dependent. Future work should test cross-cultural generalizability and improve the explainability of AI-assisted analytics.

title: Navigating Geopolitical Risk: How do Sanctions Shape Global Supply Chains?
affiliations: City University of Hong Kong, City University of Hong Kong (CityU) - Department of Economics & Finance, The Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) - CUHK Business School and Department of Finance at School of Economics (SOE),  and Wang Yanan Institute for Studies in Economics (WISE), Xiamen University

detail.title: Navigating Geopolitical Risk: How do Sanctions Shape Global Supply Chains?
detail.abstract: This study examines how firms adapt their supply chain configurations in response to US sanctions on suppliers. Using comprehensive global supply-chain data and a difference-indifferences design, we show that affected firms not only sever ties with sanctioned suppliers but also scale back relationships with nonsanctioned suppliers located in sanctioned countries, indicating spillovers of sanction risk through supplychain linkages. To bolster resilience, firms broaden their supplier bases, increase geographic diversification, relocate sourcing to countries with regional trade agreements and to nearby countries, and maintain more backup suppliers. The effects vary by firm origin: firms in sanctioned regions frequently reshore, experiencing lower profitability and sales, whereas firms in non-sanctioned regions pursue offshoring and diversification with limited financial impact. Notably, firms based in the US (the sanction sender) make fewer adjustments and are largely unaffected, with improved financial performance. By integrating political risk and economic efficiency, this study provides a framework for understanding strategic supply chain reconfiguration under geopolitical constraints, offering insights for operations research and global trade policy.

detail.abstract: Coral reefs are highly diverse and productive ecosystems that provide a wide range of ecosystem services, including recreation, coastal protection, and marine biodiversity. Climate change impacts, including ocean warming and acidification, pose a significant threat to coral reefs and the ecosystem services they provide. The variability of these impacts underlines the need to develop more spatially explicit tools in coastal ecosystem management that integrate and assess potential ecological and socio-economic outcomes. To address this, a spatially explicit predictive ecological model is applied to project changes in coral reef cover, using downscaled data from Shared Socioeconomic Pathway (SSP) climate scenarios. Based on these projections, welfare impacts of changes in recreational value are estimated across different populations and landscapes. Cumulative welfare losses for Hawaiʻi residents range from $1.5 to $3.3 billion in 2024$ by 2100. Counterintuitively, cumulative welfare losses are higher under optimistic  emissions scenarios, where coral reef degradation is less severe than higher emission scenarios, because more people will experience smaller ecological losses.  The approach incorporates site-specific characteristics, income distribution, and projected regional population growth to connect ecological change with welfare outcomes. EJScreen is used to assess variation in welfare impacts, identifying disadvantaged communities based on demographic and environmental indicators such as poverty, minority status, and exposure to environmental risks. These findings can inform policy and resource allocation by supporting ecosystem management strategies that account for both ecological dynamics and community-level socio-economic conditions.

detail.abstract: Despite an emerging body of research on online content diffusion, there has been little to no investigation of how content characteristics drive distinct temporal diffusion patterns. This study addresses this gap by investigating two primary questions: (1) What are the main diffusion patterns of online videos? (2) Which specific content characteristics influence these patterns? We estimate the Bass diffusion model on a random sample of one million YouTube videos and identify 42,046 videos with highly predictable temporal diffusion patterns. Using K-means clustering, we find that these videos fall under two broad types: (1) instant diffusion (rapid spike followed by quick decline), (2) sustained diffusion (steady growth over time). Guided by Dual Process Theory, we apply state-of-the-art machine learning methods-(1) Spotify audio analysis, (2) Whisper transcription, (3) Sentence-BERT embeddings, and (4) Topic modeling-to extract audio, visual, and textual features corresponding to System 1 (fast, emotional) versus System 2 (slow, analytical) cognitive processes. Logistic regression analyses reveal that instant diffusion is associated with high-energy, emotionally engaging content (System 1), whereas sustained diffusion is associated with informational density and complexity (System 2). Viewer engagement metrics (comment complexity, delayed sharing, longer watch times) further validate these cognitive distinctions. Our findings can be used by YouTube content creators to design video content that is tailored to achieve specific temporal viewership objectives.

detail.abstract: This case explores how academic department bylaws, an often-overlooked type of organizational document, can be used as data in qualitative content analysis. It's based on a study at a mid-sized, unionized university in the Midwest that was trying to increase faculty participation in program-level assessment. While classroom assessment is routine and tied to individual syllabi and grades, program assessment looks at whether students, as a group, have learned what a degree promises to deliver. It's a quality control mechanism, which is essential for accreditation and institutional credibility. The university had made program assessment a high-profile priority. They funded faculty travel to assessment conferences, gave out monetary awards for strong assessment plans, and offered summer stipends for faculty who wanted to improve their programs. But few faculty showed up. Participation was flat. The incentives weren't working. This led to a question: If administrators say assessment is important, is that reflected in the policies that govern what faculty get rewarded for? Using Schein's (1984) model of organizational culture, this study examined whether assessment work was embedded in departmental bylaws, the formal documents that guide promotion, tenure, and reappointment. The research involved 40 departments and more than 1,100 pages of documents. The case describes how we approached sampling, designed our categories, and handled coding decisions. Readers will learn how to conduct document-based research and explore how artefacts, like organizational documents, can reveal deeper cultural tensions within organizations. They will also come to understand that, although documents appear static and risk-free, researchers must consider the potential ethical and unintended downstream implications of their findings. Specifically, they will see how a collaborative approach using consensus coding within a summative content analysis framework can be applied to interpret complex textual data. Learning Outcomes Having read this case study, readers should be able to. . • Describe how artefacts reflect an organization's espoused and enacted values using Schein's cultural framework. • Evaluate the application of collaborative, consensus-based coding within a summative content analysis framework to accurately interpret complex and often implicit meanings in textual data. • Interpret examples of how cultural meaning can be revealed through the analysis of organizational documents. • Evaluate the ethical considerations and potential risks of conducting document-based research.

detail.abstract: Human activities increasingly disrupt ecosystems, yet the economic costs of energy infrastructure on migratory species remain underexplored. Using over 200 million GPS tracking records of migratory birds and a national database of Chinese power plants from 2014 to 2022, we show that plant construction significantly reduces bird stopover duration by 54.4% within 50 km, with effects persisting over years. Plant decommissioning generates ecological recovery, though the magnitude is smaller. We identify habitat alterations, air pollution, and water pollution as key mechanisms. By quantifying the economic consequences of energy infrastructure on migratory birds, this study advances the integration of biodiversity impacts into economic research.

detail.abstract: With the constant evolution of financial fraud techniques, the demand for advanced technological solutions to secure banking transactions and protect sensitive information is at an all-time high. For this reason, Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) have been adopted as game-changing agents in improving fraud detection and prevention. These technologies allow for real-time anomaly detection, pattern identification, and predictive analytics, revolutionizing the conventional approach to fraud detection. This article explores how AI-enabled fraud detection platforms are transforming the banking industry, specifically in the areas of cyber security, real-time transaction review, and risk management in high-frequency trading. We present a suite of new techniques to enhance the precision and proficiency of fraud detection models. Specifically, it includes the Splaso Quash Filter, a data preprocessing approach designed to optimize raw data for machine learning models, and Ripe Horn Twin Fish Optimization, a lucid feature extraction technique that improves the ability of the model to detect the critical variables affecting fraud. It uses the Adaptive Neuro Boosted Forest (ANBF) algorithm which is a combination of the neural network's adaptability and the robustness of the use of error information from the decision forest to improve the decision accuracy more than the algorithm band in the decision. We also delve into the Hash Blue Hellman Algorithm, a form of cryptography that secures the storage of data and offers a protective approach for sensitive data transactions. We discuss the implications of using AI for fraudulent activity detection, including regulatory issues, potential negative consequences, and future trends in banking fraud prevention technologies. Experimentation was conducted on the Bank Fraud Detection Dataset under a Python environment. From the analysis, it was revealed that the suggested methodology offers secure financial transactions and maintains trust in the banking industry.

detail.abstract: The Israeli strike on Qatari territory represents not only a regional escalation but also one of the gravest breaches of international norms in recent decades. Unlike prior operations in Syria, Lebanon, or Iran-where Israel justified its actions within the context of active hostilities-Qatar is neither a belligerent state nor an adversary. Instead, it functions as a U.S.-backed mediator, a pivotal global LNG supplier, and host to the largest American military base in the Middle East. Targeting such a state elevates the incident into a strategic miscalculation with systemic consequences. This paper contends that the strike constitutes a violation of international law, undermines mediation channels, and sets a perilous precedent that undermines both regional stability and the credibility of the international rules-based order. For this analysis, Third Generation Diplomacy refers to a new model of international engagement that integrates digital technologies, algorithmic governance, and ethical innovation. This concept is introduced as an alternative to outdated negotiation frameworks, highlighting the urgency of adapting diplomacy to contemporary challenges. This paper is guided by a central question: If the unraveling of the international order begins not with great-power confrontation but with the strike on a small mediator state like Qatar, what does this imply for the future of global governance and diplomacy?

detail.abstract: Announcing a large fiscal stimulus may signal the government’s pessimism about the severity of a recession to the private sector, impairing the stabilizing effects of the policy. Using a theoretical model, we show that these signaling effects occur when the stimulus exceeds expectations and are more noticeable during periods of high economic uncertainty. Analysis of a new dataset of daily stock prices and fiscal news in Japan supports these predictions. We introduce a method to identify fiscal news with different degrees of signaling effects and find that such effects weaken or, in extreme cases, even completely undermine the stabilizing impact of the announcements.

Historically, older workers were often regarded as valuable assets in traditional industrial settings due to their skills and experience. But the industrial environment is now characterized by the rapid adoption of advanced digital technologies. Older workers tend to adopt new technologies at a slower rate compared to younger generations; for firms striving to maximize productivity and competitiveness, this drawback makes the employment of older workers less attractive than in the past. 

Given the above, it is worth examining the characteristics of an aging workforce in relation to the digital transformation to produce insights that can inform industrial and workforce policy. For this study, we focus on assessing the impact of workforce aging on firms’ adoption of digital technologies. Specifically, we aim to quantitatively evaluate how the proportion of older employees within different industries affects the adoption and utilization of digital transformation technologies. Through this analysis, we seek to better understand the interaction between workforce composition and digital innovation, and ultimately offer policy insights to support a more inclusive and effective digital transition.

detail.abstract: We introduce the Cut-Based Valuation (CBV), a unified framework for consolidated value in equity/flow networks. The central idea is that economic value is never absolute: it is always defined relative to an observer Ω, which fixes perimeter, measurement basis, units/FX/PPP, discounting, informational regime, and control rules. Given Ω, the Cut Theorem shows that the consolidated value of a perimeter P depends only on boundary quantities across the cut P ↔ O, while internal reconnections are valuation-invariant. This provides (i) sufficient statistics for valuation with linear computational complexity, (ii) standardized reporting through the Perimeter-of-Validity and Cut Summary, and (iii) transformation laws that clarify how different observers relate. Applications span IFRS consolidation, national accounts, fund-of-funds, pyramids, and clearing networks, all seen as special cases of a general principle of economic relativity. Case studies (market capitalization by country, keiretsu, fund-of-funds) illustrate how CBV eliminates double counting while ensuring comparability and auditability.

detail.abstract: This chapter analyses the regime applicable to stablecoins referencing one official currency–– the e-money tokens––under the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCAR). detail.abstract: Speculative activities may serve as key triggers and accelerators of systemic financial risks. This study explores spillover effects of speculative activities across energy, financial, precious metal, and agricultural markets from a quantile-frequency perspective, and analyses drivers of their total connectedness. Key findings are as follows: first, total connectedness across the eight markets strengthens significantly under extreme speculative activities, with short-term connectedness exceeding long-term levels. Second, at the 0.05 and 0.95 quantiles, precious metals, gold in particular, act as the dominant transmitters of short-term risk shocks, driven by safe-haven demand. In contrast, oil serves as the dominant transmitter of long-term risk shocks, as its speculation is closely linked to economic fundamental trends. Meanwhile, corn and soybeans emerge as primary receivers of long-term risk shocks. Finally, five drivers show stronger predictive power for total connectedness at extreme quantiles. At high quantiles, increases in geopolitical risk (GPR), economic policy uncertainty (EPU), monetary policy uncertainty (MPU), and the consumer confidence index (CCI) inhibit short-term connectedness, due to differentiated favourable conditions and fragmented speculative motives. Conversely, increases in GPR, the stock volatility index (VIX), EPU, and MPU stimulate long-term connectedness, as speculators exploit uncertainty-induced long-term price trends to construct trading strategies.

detail.abstract: This paper introduces Non-Empirical Consistency Validation (NECV), a complementary framework for evaluating knowledge claims that resist direct empirical verification. NECV emphasizes methodological pluralism, coherence across heterogeneous sources, and increasing confidence in unverifiable claims rather than providing proof. It is operationalized through practices such as cross-cultural comparison and inclusive discussions. While NECV does not deliver final verification, it enhances plausibility and worthiness of inquiry. NECV thus expands the epistemic toolkit and broadens validation beyond empiricism, fostering rigorous yet imaginative knowledge resilient to scientific and social limitations.

detail.abstract: In an era marked by accelerating digital transformation and widening socioeconomic disparities, the relevance of physical banking infrastructure is being fundamentally redefined. This paper examines the role of hybrid branch-bank models-those that integrate digital capabilities with locally rooted, human-facing services-in restoring consumer trust and advancing retail financial inclusion. Drawing on global insights, with a particular focus on the United Kingdom, India, and underserved markets in the Global South, the paper explores how behavioural shifts, generational preferences, and environmental-social-governance (ESG) imperatives are converging to reshape expectations around access, equity, and reliability in financial services. Through a practitioner-informed lens, it considers the institutional design of inclusive banking systems, the adaptive strategies of branch networks, and the governance challenges in aligning innovation with consumer confidence. By reframing the discourse on physical versus digital as a false dichotomy, the research proposes a more nuanced model that places trust, resilience, and human-centred design at the core of banking infrastructure. The findings offer actionable insights for banks, policymakers, and financial inclusion stakeholders seeking to design sustainable, high-impact delivery models in a rapidly evolving consumer landscape.

detail.abstract: This study asks not whether to diagnose ADHD, but when, examining how diagnosis timing within the diagnosed population shapes adult labor market and health outcomes across demographic lines. Using nationally representative data from the Medical Expenditure Panel Survey (MEPS), I estimate these effects by addressing both selection on observables and unobservables through an Average Treatment Effect (ATE) framework, employing Inverse Probability Weighting (IPW), Propensity Score Matching (PSM), Double Machine Learning (DML), and an Instrumental Variable (IV). Yet, despite health gains and working 5–13% more weekly hours, early-diagnosed individuals earn less than their later-diagnosed counterparts. These findings highlight a disconnect between health and economic outcomes and emphasized the need for integrated policy approaches that combine healthcare interventions with educational and labor market supports. Policy implications are discussed.

detail.abstract: Between Bertrand and Cournot market duopoly games, it is well known that Cournot firms earn higher profit than Bertrand firms but Bertrand firms produce higher social gains than Cournot firms. We investigate the robustness of this result in the context of a liner demand and constant marginal cost model with demand size uncertainty and incomplete market research. Demand size uncertainty arises as an unknown slope of linear demand, and incomplete market research is introduced since firms' decisions are made under incomplete information about demand. Given this model specification, we show that for any degree of product substitutability (except for the case of homogeneous products), Bertrand firms dominate Cournot firms in expected equilibrium profit, consumer surplus and total surplus when there is a sufficiently high degree of demand size uncertainty. As a result, typical trade-off results between private gains (profit) and social gains do not arise between Bertrand and Cournot games. We show that Cournot firms face a higher price elasticity Bertrand firms when there is a high enough degree of demand size uncertainty. With heightened competitive pressure due to high price elasticity, Cournot firms suffer more revenue loss and thus profit in equilibrium than Bertrand firms. Finally, we show that if demand uncertainty is introduced as a parallel shift of linear demand, then Bertrand firms cannot have their expected equilibrium profit more than Cournot firms, and Cournot firms' expected price elasticity cannot exceed Bertrand firms' expected price elasticity. Remarkably, this result holds for general joint probability distributions which produce an interior equilibrium in both Bertrand and Cournot games in which non-negative price and output constraints do not bind.

detail.abstract: Biodiversity loss is now commonly recognised as a distinct source of financial risk, with transmission, measurement, and pricing properties that overlap with-but are neither reducible nor identical to-those of climate change Recent academic and policy work highlights that biodiversity shocks can undermine firm value, credit quality and access, and sovereign stability, while also contributing to systemic financial stress. However the field as yet remains at an early stage compared to the developed literature on climate finance. In this review, we aim to synthesise the emergent literature with particular emphasis on financial market evidence and systemic-risk channels. This review (i) briefly summarises the biodiversity crisis as an ecological and economic phenomenon; (ii) introduces a working taxonomy of biodiversity-related financial risks; (iii) reviews corporate-level measures and their methodological strengths and weaknesses; (iv) overviews how biodiversity risk is priced, with particular attention to volatility, liquidity, and cross asset contagion; and (v) considers governance, disclosure, and supervisory initiatives. The paper concludes with a forward-looking research agenda.

detail.abstract:
Objective. Prior research on gun ownership and violent crime has yielded inconsistent conclusions, largely because nearly all studies rely on proxy measures of prevalence-surveys, state level aggregates, or policy classifications-that cannot isolate handgun ownership, cannot confirm lawful versus illicit possession, and are vulnerable to confounding. For example, Kleck (1997) and Cook & Ludwig (2006) highlighted measurement error as the main barrier to inference, Siegel et al. (2014) reported positive associations using household survey proxies, and Donohue et al. (2019) found liberalized right-to-carry regimes associated with higher violent crime, but with treatment defined as legal regime type rather than actual prevalence. As the National Research Council concluded in its landmark 2004 review, available studies were too compromised by proxy limitations and unmeasured confounders to provide reliable evidence of causal effects. 

Design. This study is the first to eliminate that uncertainty by restricting analysis to U.S. jurisdictions that publish auditable, administrative counts of active resident handgun licenses. We constructed two cohorts: A (higher licensing prevalence, mean ≈ 10.7% of residents) and B (lower prevalence, ≤1.6%). We then compared two-year (2023-2024) totals for homicide, rape, robbery, and aggravated assault per 100,000 residents, with covariates for poverty (%), sworn law enforcement staffing (LEO per 100,000) and population density. We estimated cohort means and rate ratios, Pearson correlations with Fisher-z intervals, OLS slopes of violent rate on licensing share, and Poisson GLMs with log(population) offsets to report percent change per +1-percentage point increase in licensed share. 

Results. Mean violent crime was ≈ 542 per 100,000 in Cohort A versus ≈ 1,238 per 100,000 in Cohort B (rate ratio ≈ 2.28, 95% CI 1.52-3.43). Each +1-percentage point increase in licensing share corresponded to ≈ 7.6% lower violent incidence (IRR 0.924; 95% CI 0.890-0.958), or ≈ 60-70 fewer incidents per 100,000 depending on model specification. Adjusting for poverty or LEO staffing attenuated but did not eliminate the association. Population density was negatively correlated. Sensitivity analyses excluding outliers (Flint, MI and Washington, DC) yielded consistent results. 

Conclusions. This study is the first to demonstrate, using clean administrative licensing exposure measures, that higher lawful handgun ownership prevalence is strongly and inversely associated with personal violent crime. The association is robust across models and covariates, survives outlier tests, and directly addresses the measurement weaknesses that have limited prior scholarship. Unlike advocacy-sponsored work, this study is independent, fully transparent, and reproducible, providing the strongest evidence to date that lawful handgun prevalence aligns with substantially lower violent crime rates. We emphasize correlation rather than causation, highlight demographic, lifestyle and illicit-market limitations, and provide a reproducibility appendix with administrative URLs to support independent audit.

detail.abstract:
Humans are story telling animals, but that fact has been overlooked in one of the most fundamental of administrative law processes - notice and comment rulemaking. In this first ever survey of stories in rulemaking comments, we show how many different types of commenters are telling different types of stories for a variety of reasons. Given that stories are how humans structure reality, build social relations, and persuade each other, it is inevitable that rulemaking is full of acts of storytelling. While there has been some limited recognition of the importance of agencies listening to stories, this is not enough. Listening to stories can make agencies more knowledgeable, more representative, and more empathetic. But stories also need to be evaluated. By building on the expertise of individuals and professionals, administrative agencies can develop the expertise to evaluate stories. Overall, recognising the storied reality of rulemaking is about recognising that rulemaking was designed to be a form of legal civics. That original logic has been overlooked because of the flawed assumptions that administrative lawyers make about the purpose of rulemaking. Reinvigorating the idea of rulemaking as legal civics is particularly important in the troubled times we are in.

detail.abstract: Amid the global digitalization, government smart transformation has become a critical initiative to enhance policy-making and strengthen public service capabilities. Yet, scant attention is given to its role in government ecological policy orientation (GEPO). Drawing on panel data from 31 provincial-level regions in China from 2015 to 2023, this study systematically evaluates the impact of government smart transformation on GEPO. The findings reveal that: (1) Government smart transformation significantly improves the GEPO of Chinese local governments, reflected in stronger policy attention to ecological issues. This effect occurs through reinforcing three institutional capacities—information identification, organizational execution, and political responsiveness. Heterogeneity analyses show the effect is stronger under higher central environmental inspection pressure, fiercer inter-jurisdictional performance competition, and greater economic resource abundance. (2) Further analyses show that government smart transformation encourages local governments to prioritize environmental policy domains with greater technological feasibility and higher public salience, such as pollution control. It also renders the expression of GEPO more objective and rational. Moreover, the impact of government smart transformation on GEPO is markedly amplified at the beginning and end of local government leaders’ administrative tenures. (3) Economic impact tests demonstrate that the institutional restructuring of GEPO not only reinforces the consistency of governmental actions in ecological governance, but also fosters regional industrial upgrading and green technological innovation through spillover effects. This study reveals how government smart transformation systematically reshapes the mechanisms underlying GEPO and further elucidates its institutional pathways through which it influences policy tool selection, resource allocation, and green development outcomes.

detail.abstract: In this article, Professor Pomp examines the feasibility of implementing a state-level wealth tax and argues that such a tax would not be possible to administer effectively. The analysis identifies three central challenges: asset discovery, valuation, and taxpayer mobility. Specifically, Professor Pomp highlights the difficulty of asset discovery when ownership can be blurred through multiple trusts, LLCs, LLPs, cross-ownership, and dancing around attribution rules. Valuation presents a second challenge because of the difficulty of valuing interests in hedge funds and private equity, family corporations and partnerships, art, illiquid real estate, and complicated forms of intellectual property. Furthermore, even honest appraisers would be hard pressed to value many of the assets held by the mega-billionaires. A third challenge arises from mobility: the residency games that now take place when the stakes are relatively less substantial would intensify under a state wealth tax, eroding state revenue. While acknowledging that a federal wealth tax would face similar hurdles, Professor Pomp concludes that a state should not get out ahead of a wealth tax because failure at the state level could possibly undercut support for a federal wealth tax.

title: Fiscal Risk-Sharing
affiliations: University of Alabama - School of Law

detail.title: Fiscal Risk-Sharing
detail.abstract:
This paper argues that taxation can be seen as a form of insurance by incentivizing certain behaviors and penalizing others, thereby providing a safety net against potential risks, provided the penalties and incentives are set at an optimal level to effectively influence taxpayer behavior. For example, tax credits for renewable energy investments or health savings accounts encourage individuals and businesses to engage in actions that reduce long-term societal costs, such as environmental damage or healthcare expenses. Conversely, taxes or penalties on harmful activities, like carbon emissions or tobacco use, serve as a deterrent while generating funds that can be used to mitigate the effects of those behaviors, such as funding environmental restoration or public health programs. When the penalties and incentives are calibrated correctly, taxation acts as a mechanism to nudge taxpayers toward more socially beneficial behaviors, while also providing compensation for the risks and losses associated with negative behaviors, ultimately reducing the long-term burden on society.

Taking innovation as a case study, innovation tax incentives function as instruments of public-private partnership by leveraging private investment to advance public goals while strategically distributing financial responsibility. By offering tax measures such as credits, deductions, or accelerated expensing, the tax system encourages firms to commit capital at risk toward socially beneficial activities—such as investment in innovation infrastructure and research. Alas, when these levels are not set optimally and are not coupled with efforts to ensure accountability and penalties for non-compliance, they lose their effectiveness and devolve into corporate handouts.

The article advocates that carefully designed tax system can be utilized effectively as risk sharing apparatus as it can foster aligned financial incentives, ensuring that private actors have a stakeholder accountability in outcomes rather than acting solely as passive beneficiaries of public subsidies. In doing so, the government effectively shares the cost of policy implementation with market participants who possess specialized expertise, while promoting risk-bearing positions that internalize a portion of the uncertainty and cost associated with public goods, such as innovation and environmental protection. Through an optimal carrot-and-stick approach, tax policy not only mobilizes private resources but also enhances policy effectiveness, accountability, and social welfare.

detail.abstract: Nearly half of young children in low-and middle-income countries fail to reach their developmental potential by age five, and disparities are particularly stark in Latin America. Parenting interventions have been proven to enhance early childhood development (ECD) in specific domains; however, traditional in-person models are costly and challenging to scale. This paper reviews the growing evidence on digital parenting programs in the region, including those using SMS, WhatsApp, mobile apps, and emerging AI-based tools. Experimental studies have demonstrated that low-cost digital tools can enhance parental engagement, alleviate stress, and, in some cases, improve children's cognitive and language outcomes. However, most evaluations remain limited by small samples, short time horizons, and scarce evidence on child-level impacts or long-term effects. We highlight the challenges of engagement, equity, and scalability, and present the Chat2Learn program in Peru, a next-generation model that leverages conversational AI. We conclude with recommendations for rigorous evaluations, hybrid delivery models, and embedding digital parenting supports into government systems.

detail.abstract:
If racial gaps in measures of human capital like educational attainment and standardized test scores were eliminated, what would happen to racial disparities in wages, employment, and other labor market outcomes? A credible answer to this question is foundational for understanding the nature and scope of racial inequality and discrimination in the United States. This article reviews and synthesizes a literature that studies this question by estimating the extent to which controlling for measures of human capital changes Black-white gaps in labor market outcomes, and discusses various conceptual and methodological issues related to interpreting this type of exercise. I show that while accurately interpreting this exercise and its many variants requires careful thinking, the results elucidate many important and subtle aspects of racial inequality in the United States.

detail.abstract: In this paper, we analyze the effects of uncertainty shocks on portfolio flows in 25 emerging market and 21 advanced economies and shed light on socio-economic characteristics that may be relevant for the country-specific sensitivity towards the shocks. We derive uncertainty shocks from a proxy SVAR model, where the uncertainty shock is identified by changes in the price of gold during selected events. Taking into account the structural shock, we employ local projections of investment fund flows into 25 emerging market and 21 advanced economies for the period 2005M8 to 2023M12. Our results show that uncertainty shocks have much stronger negative effects on capital flows in emerging economies for both bond and equity flows. Our results also show that bond fund flows are much more strongly affected by uncertainty shocks compared to equity flows over both the short and the medium run. Finally, we find that economic characteristics relating to the sensitivity towards the shock differ across advanced economies and emerging markets.

detail.abstract:
The analysis highlights the Russian Federation’s instrumentalisation of the energy “weapon” as a means to change the negotiation framework with the West over the Ukraine conflict, focusing on Moscow’s oil exports.

In this respect, the study highlights the central position that the economic exploitation of this resource has in establishing a reliable budgetary year, and, as a result, in financing the war effort. At the same time, the analysis considers the effect of the sanctions imposed by the United States, the European Union and their allies on the economic ‘geography’ of oil exports, highlighting the alteration of traditional supply chains and the reconfiguration of the way in which the Russian Federation operates on global energy markets, in the context of a quantitative and qualitative metamorphosis of privileged destinations.

At the geo-economic level, the study addresses the medium- and long-term strategic sustainability of such a new export model – with a significant increase in volumes shipped to China, India, Turkey, and a few other circumstantial recipients – at a time when Moscow’s interdependence with its Asian partners is not a comfortable development in the face of considerable discounts and a price ceiling that is expected at the G7 level.

publicationDetails.detailsText: ECB Working Paper No. 2025/3108

detail.abstract: In contrast to the conventional Fisherian view that inflation reduces real debt positions, we show that significant increases in inflation are strongly associated with financial crises. In the spirit of Jordà et al. (2020), countries with free and fixed ex-change rates can be compared to difference out the confounding reaction of monetary policy. Across a dataset of 18 advanced economies over 151 years, we show that the impact of inflation extends beyond its indirect effect via monetary policy. To further corroborate causality, we instrument inflation with oil supply shocks, finding that a 1pp rise in inflation doubles the probability of financial crisis from its sample average. We give evidence for the redistribution channel, where inflationary shocks directly cut real incomes, as a possible mechanism. In conjunction with recent literature on the dangers of rapidly tightening monetary policy, our results point to a difficult trade-off for central banks once inflation has risen.

detail.abstract:
Entrepreneurs are known to be key drivers of economic growth, and the rise of online platforms and the broader "gig economy" has led self-employment to surge in recent decades. Yet the young and small businesses associated with this activity are often absent from economic data. In this paper, we explore a novel longitudinal dataset that covers the owners of tens of millions of the smallest businesses: those without employees. We produce three new sets of statistics on the rapidly growing set of nonemployer businesses. First, we measure transitions between self-employment and wage and salary jobs. Second, we describe nonemployer business entry and exit, as well as transitions between legal form (e.g., sole proprietorship to S corporation). Finally, we link owners to their nonemployer businesses and examine the dynamics of business ownership.

publicationDetails.detailsText: European Journal of Law and Economics, 0[10.1007/s10657-025-09852-0]

detail.abstract: Using the latent multidimensional approach, the paper examines the relationship between a company's legal form and its performance. Based on 72,596 observations of companies operating in Poland, we show that the legal form has a strong relationship with the company's efficiency. We reveal that the corporate form and limited liability, contrary to popular opinion, do not ensure the highest efficiency. They also do not stand out in terms of growth and risk. Entrepreneurship, direct involvement with the company, and the specific bond between partners are still key success factors. We also show that companies that are obliged to appoint governing bodies, favouring the separation of owners from management, are less efficient than those that do not have such an obligation. As a result, joint-stock companies, widely regarded as the pinnacle of the legal form, are characterized by lower efficiency than unlimited liability companies. We indicate that the reason is high agency costs, and this is confirmed by the cash ratio, used to approximate agency costs.

detail.title: Insuring Labor Income Shocks: The Role of the Dynasty

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34253
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
We provide empirical evidence on the importance of a relatively understudied channel of insurance against labor income shocks: transfers from (cash-rich) parents to (cash-short) children when the latter experience negative wage shocks. Matching population data for Norway across two generations, we establish several results. First, parents make a transfer—i.e., run down liquid assets—when adult children experience negative labor income shocks. Consistent with dynastic insurance, we observe no transfers when income shocks are positive. Second, parents' responses depend on the nature of the shock. If losses are temporary, parents dissave; if they are persistent, parents save in order to make future transfers. Parental transfers offset 43% of temporary and 27% of persistent losses. Third, insurance is lower when children have other smoothing options, like spousal labor supply, and is greater for shocks to their own child versus a child’s spouse. Support also increases if the spouse’s parents can contribute, suggesting “competition for attention.” Lastly, insurance flows are one-way: children do not insure their parents against income losses.

detail.title: How People Use ChatGPT

publicationDetails.detailsText: NBER Working Paper No. w34255
publicationDetails.journalName: NBER Working Paper Series

detail.abstract:
Despite the rapid adoption of LLM chatbots, little is known about how they are used. We document the growth of ChatGPT’s consumer product from its launch in November 2022 through July 2025, when it had been adopted by around 10% of the world’s adult population. Early adopters were disproportionately male but the gender gap has narrowed dramatically, and we find higher growth rates in lower-income countries. Using a privacy-preserving automated pipeline, we classify usage patterns within a representative sample of ChatGPT conversations. We find steady growth in work-related messages but even faster growth in non-work-related messages, which have grown from 53% to more than 70% of all usage. Work usage is more common for educated users in highly-paid professional occupations. We classify messages by conversation topic and find that “Practical Guidance,” “Seeking Information,” and “Writing” are the three most common topics and collectively account for nearly 80% of all conversations. Writing dominates work-related tasks, highlighting chatbots’ unique ability to generate digital outputs compared to traditional search engines. Computer programming and self-expression both represent relatively small shares of use. Overall, we find that ChatGPT provides economic value through decision support, which is especially important in knowledge-intensive jobs.
